claim: Increased tonic activity of locus coeruleus noradrenergic (LC-NE) neurons induces anxiety-like and aversive behavior.
source: Increased tonic activity of locus coeruleus noradrenergic (LC-NE) neurons induces anxiety-like and aversive behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Photostimulation of LC-NE fibers in the BLA evokes norepinephrine release in the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
source: We demonstrate that photostimulation of LC-NE fibers in the BLA evokes norepinephrine release in the basolateral amygdala (BLA)
evidence: This claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Photostimulation of LC-NE fibers in the BLA alters BLA neuronal activity.
source: We demonstrate that photostimulation of LC-NE fibers in the BLA evokes norepinephrine release in the basolateral amygdala (BLA), alters BLA neuronal activity
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Photostimulation of LC-NE fibers in the BLA conditions aversion.
source: We demonstrate that photostimulation of LC-NE fibers in the BLA evokes norepinephrine release in the basolateral amygdala (BLA), alters BLA neuronal activity, conditions aversion
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place aversion behavioral data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Photostimulation of LC-NE fibers in the BLA increases anxiety-like behavior.
source: We demonstrate that photostimulation of LC-NE fibers in the BLA evokes norepinephrine release in the basolateral amygdala (BLA), alters BLA neuronal activity, conditions aversion, and increases anxiety-like behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test and elevated zero maze behavioral data presented in Figure 6.

claim: β-adrenergic receptors mediate the anxiety-like phenotype of increased NE release in the BLA.
source: Additionally, we report that β-adrenergic receptors mediate the anxiety-like phenotype of increased NE release in the BLA.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological blockade experiments with propranolol presented in Figure 6G.

claim: The LC sends projections to the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
source: This non-selective retrograde tracing approach revealed known inputs into the BLA from the LC (Robertson et al., 2016; Asan, 1998; Fallon et al., 1978) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1B and cited prior literature.

claim: Th+ LC neurons project terminal fibers to the BLA.
source: Here we clearly observed labeled LC neurons (Figure 1F and G) and their projection fibers terminating in the BLA (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: Photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 projections results in NE release at terminals.
source: Using the same viral optogenetic strategy as above, we examined whether photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 projections resulted in NE release at terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data presented in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Photostimulation of BLA slices produces characteristic cyclic voltammograms and uptake consistent with NE.
source: Photostimulation of BLA slices, produced characteristic cyclic voltammograms and uptake consistent with NE (McElligott et al., 2013; Herr et al., 2012) (t1/2 = 2.0 ± 0.2 s, Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltammetry data shown in Figure 2C-D and cited prior literature on NE detection methods.

claim: Reserpine treatment significantly attenuates optically-evoked oxidative currents in the BLA.
source: Reserpine treatment significantly attenuated the measured oxidative currents (31.6 ± 1.0% of baseline, Figure 2E and F) further confirming optically-evoked catecholamine release in this isolated ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 projection.
evidence: This claim is supported by reserpine treatment data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 terminals causes an increase in firing frequency in 21.4% of BLA units recorded.
source: In these experiments photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 terminals caused an increase in firing frequency in 21.4% of units recorded in the BLA (Figure 3C–E,H; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C-E, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 terminals causes inhibitory responses in 9.5% of BLA units recorded.
source: while some cells (9.5%) displayed inhibitory responses (Figure 3D,F,I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3D, F, I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 69.0% of BLA neurons did not change firing in response to photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 terminals.
source: The remaining neurons (69.0%) appeared to not change in response to photostimulation (Figure 3D,G,J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3D, G, J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mean latency to fire following each light pulse in neurons that increased firing was 129.3 ± 108.9 ms.
source: In cases where the firing rate increased, the mean ± SD latency to fire following each light pulse was 129.3 ± 108.9 ms, suggesting that this change is not due to fast, monosynaptic neurotransmission, but likely a polysynaptic and/or neuromodulatory effect (Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by latency analysis data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The change in firing rate is not due to fast, monosynaptic neurotransmission, but likely a polysynaptic and/or neuromodulatory effect.
source: In cases where the firing rate increased, the mean ± SD latency to fire following each light pulse was 129.3 ± 108.9 ms, suggesting that this change is not due to fast, monosynaptic neurotransmission, but likely a polysynaptic and/or neuromodulatory effect (Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the latency data shown in Figure 3K, which shows relatively long latencies inconsistent with monosynaptic transmission.

claim: 5 Hz photostimulation increases cFos expression within the BLA in ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2+ animals compared to ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2- controls.
source: Photostimulation of LC-NE terminals in the BLA (5 Hz, 10 ms) significantly increases the number of cFos-expressing BLA neurons in ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 animals compared to ChR2-lacking (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: cFos expression following LC-NE terminal activation in the BLA overlaps significantly more with vHPC- and CeA-targeted CTB compared to NAc-targeted CTB in the BLA.
source: These immunohistochemistry studies reveal that the cFos present following LC-NE terminal activation in the BLA, overlaps significantly more with vHPC- and CeA-targeted compared to NAc-targeted CTB in the BLA (Figure 4C–G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C-G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: LC-NE terminals in the BLA preferentially activate vHPC- and CeA- projecting BLA neurons thought to be involved in modulating negative valence and affective behaviors.
source: These results suggest that LC-NE terminals in the BLA preferentially activate vHPC- and CeA- projecting BLA neurons thought to be involved in modulating negative valence and affective behaviors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cFos overlap data in Figure 4 and knowledge about the role of vHPC and CeA projections in negative affect.

claim: Photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 terminals using parameters that induce a real-time place aversion at LC-NE cell bodies failed to elicit a real-time aversion in ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 animals.
source: Surprisingly, photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 terminals using the parameters that induce a real-time place aversion at LC-NE cell bodies (McCall et al., 2015) failed to elicit a real-time aversion in ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 animals (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by real-time place testing data shown in Figure 5B-C and comparison to prior work cited.

claim: There was no significant change in place testing behavior or locomotor behavior within animals or compared to ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:eYFP controls at either 5 Hz or 60 Hz photostimulation.
source: There was no significant change in place testing behavior (Figure 5C) or locomotor behavior (Figure 5D) within animals or compared to ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:eYFP controls at either a physiologically-relevant 5 Hz or an over-driven 60 Hz photostimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The real-time negative valence of LC-NE stimulation is likely produced via another LC-NE projection and one that is not recruited through antidromic stimulation of BLA-projecting LC neurons.
source: These results indicate that the real-time negative valence of LC-NE stimulation is likely produced via another LC-NE projection and one that is not recruited through antidromic stimulation of BLA-projecting LC neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of real-time place aversion in LC-BLA terminal stimulation experiments compared to prior cell body stimulation results.

claim: ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 mice show a conditioned aversive response to chamber paired with photostimulation compared to ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:eYFP controls following two days of conditioning.
source: When allowed to freely explore two contextually-differentiated chambers, following two conditioning days of photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 terminals (5 Hz, 10 ms), animals expressing ChR2-eYFP spent significantly less time in the context that was previously paired with photostimulation compared to the ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:eYFP controls (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioned place aversion data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: Neither ChR2 nor eYFP control mice showed significant changes in locomotor activity before, during, or after conditioning in the CPA assay.
source: Neither group of mice showed significant changes in locomotor activity before, during, or after conditioning (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Stimulation of LC-BLA fibers alone is sufficient to cause a conditioned aversion.
source: Following the observation that stimulation of LC-BLA fibers alone is sufficient to cause a conditioned aversion
evidence: This claim is supported by the conditioned place aversion data in Figure 5.

claim: 5 Hz photostimulation causes an anxiety-like phenotype in OFT of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 animals compared to ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:eYFP controls.
source: Photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 terminals using parameters that induce anxiety-like behavior at LC-NE cell bodies (McCall et al., 2015) resulted in a significant decrease in time spent in the center of the open field (OFT) with no significant change in general locomotor activity (Figure 6A–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 6A-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Stimulation of only the subset of LC-NE fibers that project to the BLA is sufficient to induce anxiety-like behaviors.
source: These experiments suggest that stimulation of only the subset of LC-NE fibers that project to the BLA is sufficient to induce anxiety-like behaviors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the open field test data showing anxiety-like behavior with LC-BLA terminal stimulation.

claim: 5 Hz photostimulation causes an anxiety-like phenotype in EZM of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 animals compared to ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:eYFP controls, which is reversed by intra-BLA propranolol pretreatment.
source: The same photostimulation paradigm that was anxiogenic in the OFT, caused a decrease in time spent in the open area of the elevated zero maze (EZM) of ChR2+ animals that received vehicle, compared to YFP-expressing, vehicle controls (Figure 6G and H). Importantly, when we locally antagonized β-ARs directly in the BLA prior to photostimulation, anxiogenesis was completely blocked in ChR2+ animals with no effect on eYFP-expressing, propranolol controls (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by elevated zero maze data with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: Local β-AR activation by NE release from LC-BLA terminals is the substrate responsible for the photostimulation-induced anxiety-like behavior.
source: These findings suggest that local β-AR activation by NE release from LC-BLA terminals is the substrate responsible for the photostimulation-induced anxiety-like behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the propranolol blockade data in Figure 6G showing that β-AR antagonism prevents anxiety-like behavior.

claim: The BLA is a crucial component in the neural circuitry of negative affective behaviors.
source: The BLA is a crucial component in the neural circuitry of negative affective behaviors (Davis, 1992; Davidson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of BLA cell bodies and their projections can bidirectionally mediate anxiety-like behavior and fear encoding.
source: Activation of BLA cell bodies and their projections can bidirectionally mediate anxiety-like behavior and fear encoding (Davis, 1992; Kim et al., 2013; Tye et al., 2011; Namburi et al., 2015; Beyeler et al., 2016; Wolff et al., 2014; Knoll et al., 2011; Crowley et al., 2016; Sears et al., 2013; Roozendaal et al., 2006; Felix-Ortiz et al., 2013; Debiec and Ledoux, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NE is increased in the BLA following stressful events.
source: NE is increased in the BLA following stressful events (Galvez et al., 1996; Hatfield et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The BLA receives noradrenergic input from the LC as well the Hoxb1+ neuronal populations in the lower brainstem and NTS.
source: The BLA receives noradrenergic input from the LC (Asan, 1998; Fallon et al., 1978) as well the Hoxb1+ neuronal populations in the lower brainstem and NTS (Robertson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The LC input to the BLA is less dense than other NE input.
source: Despite the LC input being less dense than other NE input (Plummer et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Molecularly-defined Th+ positive fibers from the LC release catecholamines into the amygdala and alter behavior.
source: here we directly show that molecularly-defined Th+ positive fibers from the LC release catecholamines into the amygdala and alter behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by the voltammetry and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Noradrenergic tonic cell firing in the LC increases following stressful stimuli.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that noradrenergic tonic cell firing in the LC increases following stressful stimuli (McCall et al., 2015; Abercrombie and Jacobs, 1987a, 1987b; Aston-Jones et al., 1999; Mana and Grace, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Selective activation of Th+ LC terminals modulates BLA neuronal activity in vivo.
source: We now demonstrate that selective activation of Th+ LC terminals from these neurons modulates BLA neuronal activity in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vivo electrophysiology data in Figure 3.

claim: Neurons that increase firing to LC-BLA photostimulation have a higher probability of being BLA projection neurons.
source: Despite a diversity of recorded responses, these findings align with prior studies suggesting neurons that increase firing to LC-BLA photostimulation have a higher probability of being BLA projection neurons, while those that decrease have a higher probability of being BLA interneurons (Figure 3L) (Likhtik et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the baseline firing rate data in Figure 3L and cited prior literature on BLA neuron types.

claim: Neurons that decrease firing to LC-BLA photostimulation have a higher probability of being BLA interneurons.
source: Despite a diversity of recorded responses, these findings align with prior studies suggesting neurons that increase firing to LC-BLA photostimulation have a higher probability of being BLA projection neurons, while those that decrease have a higher probability of being BLA interneurons (Figure 3L) (Likhtik et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the baseline firing rate data in Figure 3L and cited prior literature on BLA neuron types.

claim: Activation of β-ARs increases BLA activity.
source: Though it is well established that activation of β-ARs increases BLA activity (Buffalari and Grace, 2007; Huang et al., 1996; Pu et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The diversity of neuronal responses observed are likely mediated through different receptors systems and/or local or distal polysynaptic recurrent circuitry.
source: Indeed, it is likely that the diversity of neuronal responses we observed are mediated through different receptors systems (Buffalari and Grace, 2007) and/or local or distal polysynaptic recurrent circuitry (Wolff et al., 2014; Rosenkranz and Grace, 2002, 1999).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed data and cited prior literature.

claim: NE serves to preferentially shift BLA activity in neurons that favor anxiety-like behavior rather than those that favor positive affect and anxiolysis.
source: Furthermore, while we do not know the genetic identity or projection targets of the BLA neurons from which we recorded, it is possible that NE serves to preferentially shift BLA activity in neurons that favor anxiety-like behavior (i.e. those that project to the ventral hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, or central amygdala) rather those that favor positive affect and anxiolysis (i.e. projections to the nucleus accumbens and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis)(Kim et al., 2013; Stuber et al., 2011; Tye et al., 2011; Namburi et al., 2015; Beyeler et al., 2016; Felix-Ortiz et al., 2013, 2016; Felix-Ortiz and Tye, 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the cFos data and cited prior literature on BLA projection targets.

claim: cFos is a secondary marker for neuronal excitation.
source: The combined retrograde labeling and photostimulation studies indicate that, cFos, a secondary marker for neuronal excitation (Madabhushi et al., 2015), is selectively increased in the CeA- and vHPC-projecting BLA neurons (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Increasing the activity of CaMKII+ BLA neurons via chemogenetic or optogenetic activation of Gαs-signaling produces an anxiogenic-like state.
source: Furthermore, our recent reports demonstrate that increasing the activity of CaMKII+ BLA neurons via chemogenetic or optogenetic activation of Gαs-signaling also produces an anxiogenic-like state, suggesting that excitatory cells possibly mediate the LC-BLA noradrenergic effect (Siuda et al., 2015a, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The conditioned aversive behavior may be due to factors outside of the BLA and distinct from NE release such as antidromic activity at the LC cell bodies or from prolonged changes to LC circuit activity elsewhere.
source: However, it remains to be seen whether this conditioned aversive behavior is mediated locally in the BLA by NE. This effect may could be due to factors outside of the BLA and distinct from NE release such as antidromic activity at the LC cell bodies or from prolonged changes to LC circuit activity elsewhere that result from long-term, repeated optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about alternative explanations for the observed conditioned aversion.

claim: Prolonged NE release in the BLA modulates memory storage through β-AR-mediated cAMP production and this effect is regulated by α1-AR and α2-AR activity.
source: It is well established that prolonged NE release in the BLA modulates memory storage through β-AR-mediated cAMP production and this effect, in turn, is regulated by α1-AR and α2-AR activity (Galvez et al., 1996; Hatfield et al., 1999; Liang et al., 1990; Ferry and McGaugh, 2008; Ferry et al., 1999a, 1999b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Noradrenergic signaling in the BLA influences fear-related memory formation.
source: In particular, many groups have shown noradrenergic influence in fear-related memory formation (Sears et al., 2013; Roozendaal et al., 2008, 2006; Debiec and Ledoux, 2004; Garrido Zinn et al., 2016; Skelly et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The LC-BLA circuitry carries an intrinsically negative valence.
source: The observation that the LC-BLA circuitry carries an intrinsically negative valence suggests that this circuit can natively promote negative affect, rather than merely enhancing memory.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the conditioned place aversion data.

claim: The anxiety-like phenotype can be blocked with local β-AR antagonism.
source: While there is some concern that photostimulation of ThIRES-Cre::LC-BLA:ChR2 fibers could cause backpropagating action potentials to LC-NE cell bodies resulting in NE release elsewhere in the brain for the conditioned place aversion, the observation that the anxiety-like phenotype can be blocked with local β-AR antagonism (Figure 6G) suggests there is some degree of circuit isolation in our study.
evidence: This claim is supported by the propranolol blockade data in Figure 6G.

claim: Photostimulation of LC-BLA terminals does not replicate all of the behavioral phenotypes of cell body activation.
source: Additionally, the observation that this stimulation does not replicate all of the behavioral phenotypes of cell body activation (McCall et al., 2015) (Figure 5C; i.e. no RTPA) further supports this interpretation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lack of real-time place aversion in Figure 5C compared to prior cell body stimulation results.

claim: Gαs signaling in CaMKIIα+ BLA neurons is sufficient for anxiogenesis, without driving either a real-time or conditioned place aversion.
source: To this point, we recently demonstrated that Gαs signaling (the same signaling mechanism that β-AR activates) in CaMKIIα+ BLA neurons is sufficient for anxiogenesis, without driving either a real-time or conditioned place aversion (Siuda et al., 2015a, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: LC neurons with fibers in the BLA are capable of conditioning aversion, though possibly through other brain regions and possibly independent of β-AR activation.
source: Together with our work at LC-NE cell bodies (McCall et al., 2015), these studies and the current findings suggest that LC neurons with fibers in the BLA are capable of conditioning aversion, though possibly through other brain regions and possibly independent of β-AR activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of the current study and prior work.

claim: The real-time place aversion elicited by LC-NE cell body activation is dependent on α1-AR activation.
source: We previously demonstrated the real-time place aversion elicited by LC-NE cell body activation to be dependent on α1-AR activation (McCall et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The anatomical substrate and receptor system responsible for real-time place aversion is distinct from the efferent LC-NE processes responsible for noradrenergic mediated anxiety-like behavior.
source: Together these results suggest that both the anatomical substrate and receptor system responsible for this behavior is distinct from the efferent LC-NE processes responsible for noradrenergic mediated anxiety-like behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential behavioral and pharmacological results between real-time place aversion and anxiety-like behavior.

claim: RTPA is essentially an instrumental conditioning paradigm that relies on operant learning of the subject as it engages the environment.
source: RTPA is essentially an instrumental conditioning paradigm that relies on operant learning of the subject as it engages the environment, while CPA is a passive, classical conditioning paradigm that possibly recruit distinct brain circuitry during the learning process (Day and Carelli, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and general knowledge about behavioral paradigms.

claim: CPA is a passive, classical conditioning paradigm that possibly recruit distinct brain circuitry during the learning process.
source: RTPA is essentially an instrumental conditioning paradigm that relies on operant learning of the subject as it engages the environment, while CPA is a passive, classical conditioning paradigm that possibly recruit distinct brain circuitry during the learning process (Day and Carelli, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and general knowledge about behavioral paradigms.

claim: NE has slower temporal dynamics compared to fast-acting, small molecule neurotransmitters, such as GABA and glutamate.
source: Another consideration is the longer time course of NE transmission and receptor activation compared to fast-acting, small molecule neurotransmitters, such as γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glutamate (Otis and Mody, 1992; Isaacson et al., 1993; Zoli et al., 1998; Szapiro and Barbour, 2007; Agnati et al., 2010; Palij and Stamford, 1994; Courtney and Ford, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: β-AR signaling through cAMP-gated calcium channels can increase firing acutely.
source: It is well known, for example, that β-AR signaling through cAMP-gated calcium channels that will likely increase firing acutely
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about β-AR signaling mechanisms.

claim: β-AR signaling through Arrestin-mediated transduction can lead to long-term changes in gene and protein expression in addition to changes synaptic plasticity and neuronal activity.
source: but that they also signal through Arrestin-mediated transduction. The latter can lead to long-term changes in gene and protein expression in addition to changes synaptic plasticity and neuronal activity (Siuda et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and established knowledge about β-AR signaling.

claim: The LC sends functional projections to the dopaminergic system.
source: The LC sends functional projections to the dopaminergic system
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Numerous groups have demonstrated bidirectional control of real-time place preference and aversion behaviors within the mesolimbic dopamine system.
source: and numerous groups have demonstrated bidirectional control of real-time place preference and aversion behaviors within this system (Siuda et al., 2015b; Jennings et al., 2013; Lammel et al., 2012; Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012; Isingrini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: LC-NE downstream influence on negative affective behaviors is an elaborate and complex system likely involving many different postsynaptic receptor systems and anatomical projection targets.
source: Taken together, our results here and elsewhere (McCall et al., 2015; Siuda et al., 2015a, 2016) demonstrate that LC-NE downstream influence on negative affective behaviors is an elaborate and complex system likely involving many different postsynaptic receptor systems and anatomical projection targets.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion inferred from the current study and cited prior work.

claim: The LC projection to the BLA is a clear functional efferent target for LC-mediated anxiety-like behavior.
source: Importantly, the LC projection to the BLA is a clear functional efferent target for LC-mediated anxiety-like behavior.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.
